---
title: The regeneration contract
description: Contracts regenerate freely. Your code is never touched. That's the whole deal.
---

A codegen tool you can't re-run is a scaffolding tool. The point of webmcp-codegen is that
your API keeps evolving and your tools keep up — so the merge behavior is the most carefully
designed part of the whole thing.

## One file, two regions

Every per-tool file is split by marker lines:

```ts
import { getModelContext } from "./runtime.webmcp";

// ─── webmcp-codegen: generated — do not edit this region ───
// name, description, input schema, input type, hints, register()
// …derived from your spec, refreshed on every generate…
// ─── webmcp-codegen: end generated — your code below survives regeneration ───

export async function executeGetOrderStatus(input: GetOrderStatusInput) {
  // yours, forever
}
```

**Above the marker** is the contract: name, description, the JSON Schema advertised to the
agent, the TypeScript input type, the safety hints, the `register…()` wrapper. These track
your spec and are regenerated on every run.

**Below the marker** is `execute()`, scaffolded exactly once — when the file is first
created — and never written again. Change a description in your spec and re-run: the doc
comment updates, your implementation survives word for word.

## The rules, precisely

| Situation on re-run | What happens |
|---|---|
| New operation in the spec | New file, `create` — with a fresh `execute()` scaffold |
| Contract changed, your region intact | File updated above the marker only (`update`) |
| Nothing changed | Nothing written (`unchanged` — no diff noise in git) |
| You edited *above* the marker, or removed the markers | Your file is left alone; the new version goes to `<name>.webmcp.ts.new` and the report shows a **conflict** |

That last row is the promise in its sharpest form: webmcp-codegen would rather write a
sibling file and admit defeat than overwrite something you wrote by hand.

## Owning it

Because the output is plain TypeScript with no runtime dependency on the package, you can
stop re-generating at any point and just keep the files. "You own the output" isn't a
license question — it's an architecture property.

`runtime.webmcp.ts` and `index.ts` are the exception: they're fully regenerated every run
(their headers say so), because you should never need to edit them.

## What to commit

Commit the generated files. They're source code your app imports — like migrations or
generated API clients, they belong in review. Diffs in the contract region are also the
clearest possible signal of "the API changed, the tools follow."
